passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel cognitive training program on working memory performance in adults aged 25–35. The study employed a randomized controlled design with 120 participants, equally divided into an experimental group (receiving the training) and a control group (engaging in non-cognitive leisure activities). Over a 6‑week period, participants completed a series of standardized working memory tasks at baseline, mid‑intervention, and post‑intervention. The training consisted of adaptive n‑back exercises delivered via a computer application, while the control group participated in general educational videos. The primary outcome measure was the change in the mean working memory capacity score, calculated as the sum of correct responses across all tasks. Secondary outcomes included reaction time and self‑reported cognitive fatigue. The researchers also collected demographic data and baseline neuropsychological assessments to ensure group equivalence. The study aimed to determine whether the training could produce statistically significant improvements in working memory relative to the control condition, and to explore the durability of any gains at a 3‑month follow‑up. The control group’s mean response time was 655 ms at baseline and 650 ms post‑intervention; the experimental group’s was 650 ms at baseline and 610 ms post‑intervention.
table_data:
Group | Time point | Mean Response Time (ms) | Standard Deviation
--- | --- | --- | ---
Experimental | Baseline | 650 | 48
Experimental | Post‑Intervention | 610 | 42
Control | Baseline | 655 | 49
Control | Post‑Intervention | 650 | 50
stem: Based on the table, which of the following statements accurately reflects the mean response time for the experimental group at post‑intervention?
explanation: The table lists the mean response time for the experimental group at post‑intervention as 610 ms.
trap: Confusing the baseline mean with the post‑intervention mean for the experimental group.

stem: Which experimental design element best controls for potential confounding variables in this study?

options.A: Random assignment to experimental and control groups
options.C: Measuring reaction time as a secondary outcome

explanation: Random assignment ensures that confounding variables are evenly distributed across groups, providing the strongest control for potential confounders.
trap: Assuming that measuring reaction time automatically controls for all confounding variables.

stem: If the experimental group’s mean response time improved by 10% from baseline, what is the post‑intervention mean response time?
explanation: A 10% improvement is 0.10 x 650 = 65 ms, so post-intervention mean = 650 - 65 = 585 ms.
trap: Option C (610 ms) is the table value (a 6.2% change), not a 10% improvement.

stem: Which of the following is a common trap when interpreting the study’s results?

options.A: Concluding the training works from the experimental group's before-and-after change without comparing it with the control group's change
options.C: Using a 6‑week duration instead of 12 weeks

explanation: Correct: A) A pre-post change in the trained group alone cannot separate the training effect from practice, expectancy or time; the comparison with the control group's change is needed. Why the others are wrong: B) The table already reports SDs. C) The passage gives no reason that 12 weeks is needed. D) An age restriction limits generalizability but is not an interpretation trap.
trap: Treating the experimental group's own improvement (650 to 610 ms) as proof of an effect without checking that the control group changed much less.

stem: Which analysis best tests whether the training group improved more than the control group from baseline to post-intervention?

options.A: Group x time interaction in a repeated-measures ANOVA
options.B: Paired t-test in the training group only
options.C: Chi-square test of group and sex
options.D: Pearson correlation of age with baseline score

explanation: Differential change between groups is the group x time interaction. A paired test in one group ignores the control comparison.
trap: A within-group pre/post test cannot show the effect exceeds that of the control.
